html:
The Battle of Warsaw was fought from 12 to 25 August 1920 on the edge of Warsaw, the capital of Poland. The Polish army beat the Red Army of Soviet Russia and saved the country's new independence.

Poland had come back onto the map in 1918, and its eastern border was not settled. Its leader Józef Piłsudski advanced into Ukraine and took Kyiv in May 1920. The Red Army struck back and drove the Poles hundreds of kilometres west. Lenin hoped to carry the revolution through Poland into Germany. By August the Soviet commander Mikhail Tukhachevsky was at the gates of Warsaw, but his armies were tired and spread out, and his southern side was weak. Polish codebreakers were reading Soviet radio messages. While the city's defenders held, Piłsudski attacked from the south on 16 August. The Soviet armies fell apart. Tens of thousands of men were captured, and about 30,000 fled into East Prussia.

The Peace of Riga in 1921 fixed Poland's eastern border until 1939. The battle stopped the spread of Soviet communism into central Europe for a generation. Stalin, a commissar on the Soviet front further south, was blamed by some for not sending help.
